You pass with an iterative reversal that handles the empty list and a single node and says O(n) time and O(1) space. The same algorithm on raw

A linked list stores a sequence as separate nodes, each its own heap allocation holding a value and a pointer to the next node, rather than one contiguous block. In C++, ownership is the chain itself: each node owns the next through a
, and the variable holding the head owns the first node, so nobody ever writes
. Code that only reads the list walks it with a raw, non-owning pointer, and a function that takes the list over says so by taking the
by value, handing it back the same way.
It's rarely the right reach as a default container: each node's separate allocation defeats the processor's prefetcher, and a
, moving its elements through one contiguous block, wins even at sorted insertion, where the list's O(1) splice looks like the natural fit. The right reach for a real

is when something else holds iterators or references into it that must survive insertions and removals elsewhere, or when elements move between lists by splicing, as an LRU cache does. Outside that, linked lists mostly show up as an interview exercise in pointer surgery: reversing, merging, detecting a cycle, walking to the middle.
The mechanism worth naming is the order of moves. Rewiring a link has to take the rest of the list out of a node before that node's own link is overwritten, because a

assignment destroys whatever it already owned. A dummy node placed before the head gives the first node a predecessor, so removing it needs no separate case from removing any other node, and fast and slow pointers walk at two speeds to find a middle or a cycle in one pass with no extra memory.
The mistake that shows up under pressure is in the teardown, not the surgery: destroying a

list is recursive, because each node's destructor destroys the next one from inside itself, so a long enough list runs out of stack at the closing brace, in code a reviewer would call correct. The same shape crashes a recursive reverse or merge. The fix is a destructor, or a
, that unlinks nodes one at a time in a loop instead of letting the chain destroy itself.

You meet this in the interview question itself: reverse a singly linked list in place, reusing its nodes with no allocation and O(1) extra space, which is exactly the pointer surgery this page is about.

c.v: This program builds a list of a million nodes and does nothing wrong that a reviewer would see:
It gets as far as the closing brace of

is destroyed, and crashes there: AddressSanitizer reports a stack-overflow. As the theory showed, each node's destructor destroys the next node from inside itself, so destroying a list of n nodes nests n destructor calls. The stack is finite, 8 MB on the WSL machine these numbers come from (
prints 8192). There, with GCC 13.3 and no sanitizers, a list of 50,000 nodes was destroyed and one of 60,000 crashed at

the limit lay between 500,000 and 550,000 nodes. A robot that logs a long path in such a list crashes when it clears the log, far from any line that looks wrong. Herb Sutter's talk on leak freedom (CppCon 2016) makes the same point: destruction through owning pointers is recursive by default, and a long chain can exceed the stack.
The fix is a destructor that unlinks the nodes one at a time. It belongs in the class that owns the list:

Unique ownership can still leak, in two ways. The first is
: it gives up ownership and returns a raw pointer, and if nobody takes that pointer over, the node is lost. Transfer ownership with a move instead, which is the advice in Olsen's talk, and treat any
outside a line that hands the pointer to a new owner as a bug. The second is a cycle. Link the last node of a list back to its head, as the cycle problems do, and the ring owns itself:

LeakSanitizer, which runs with AddressSanitizer on Linux, reports at exit that 48 bytes in 3 allocations, the three 16-byte nodes, are no longer reachable. Node 3 owns node 1, node 1 owns node 2, and node 2 owns node 3, so none of their destructors can ever run. That is why a list with a cycle lives in an arena, where the vector owns the nodes and a cycle is a set of numbers.
